This page sets out what the law and the Election Commission's own orders give an elector whose name was left off the draft or the final roll, and where to get help. It is general information drawn from those documents, and it is not legal advice on any one case. The state's Chief Electoral Officer, the registration officer and the District Legal Services Authority can say how a step works in a particular state.

Listing an organisation here is not an endorsement, and leaving one out says nothing about it. If you know of an organisation that helped electors, or a listing is out of date, write to the address at the foot of the page with a link that shows it.

Ask to be put back on the roll with Form 6

If your name was left off the draft or the final roll, fill in Form 6, the application to be added to the roll. During the claims and objections period of the revision it goes with the declaration attached to it for the revision. Once the revision is over in your state you can still apply at any time under continuous updation, on the ordinary Form 6 of the 1960 Rules. Form 6A is for Indian citizens living abroad, and Form 8 is for a change of address or a mistake in your own entry.
Get Form 6 from your booth level officer (BLO), the registration officer's office, voters.eci.gov.in or the ECINet app.
During the revision, attach the declaration that goes with Form 6 for the revision.
Hand it to the BLO or the registration officer, or file it online, and keep the reference number.
Apply well before an election is called. No name can be added after the last date for nominations until that election is over.
Use Form 8 if you moved house, within the state or from another state, or if your entry has a mistake. Use Form 6A if you live abroad on an Indian passport.
Objections and the hearing before any deletion

Form 7 is the form for objecting to a name on the roll, or to a name proposed to be added. When someone objects to your name, the registration officer has to send you a notice and hear you before deciding. Before deleting a name on the ground that the person has moved away or is not entitled to be on the roll, the officer has to give that person a reasonable chance to be heard. In the revision no entry could be deleted from the draft without an inquiry and a fair chance to be heard, followed by a written order with reasons. If you get a notice, go to the hearing or send the documents asked for, and ask for the order in writing.
Check the lists of claims and objections the registration officer puts up on the notice board and the Chief Electoral Officer's website.
If someone has objected to your name, you should get a notice with the date, time and place of the hearing.
Attend in person or through someone you authorise where that is allowed, and take your documents.
Ask for the registration officer's decision in writing. You need it for an appeal.
Appeal to the District Magistrate, then to the Chief Electoral Officer

If the registration officer's decision goes against you, you can appeal to the District Magistrate under section 24 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. If the District Magistrate's order also goes against you, a second appeal lies to the state's Chief Electoral Officer. The Commission's revision order kept both appeals and gave 30 days from the District Magistrate's order for the second. The Chief Electoral Officer of Goa, in the note on its final roll, gave 15 days from the registration officer's decision for the first.
Get a copy of the registration officer's order.
Write a short appeal to the District Magistrate, signed by you, with the order attached, within 15 days of the registration officer's decision.
If it is turned down, appeal to the Chief Electoral Officer within 30 days of the District Magistrate's order.
Keep copies and receipts of everything you hand in.
The 1950 helpline, complaints, and the drive to find those left off

You can call the voter helpline on 1950, or the national toll-free number 1800-11-1950 from 8 am to 8 pm, and every complaint is logged on the National Grievance Service Portal. The ECINet app has a Book-a-Call with BLO feature, and complaints can also be emailed to complaints@eci.gov.in. After the revision, the Commission ordered BLOs to compare the roll from before the revision with the present one, visit those missing, and help anyone still eligible fill in Form 6. The lists are to be shared with the parties' booth agents, and booth level camps are to be held. Special camps may also be held for people in night shelters and labour colonies and for the homeless.
Call 1950, or 1800-11-1950, and note the complaint number.
Use Book-a-Call with BLO on the ECINet app to ask your BLO to visit.
If a BLO visits during the drive, fill in Form 6 then and there if you are eligible.
Look for booth level camps in your area, and special camps if you live in a night shelter or labour colony.
Free legal help from the legal services authorities

Under section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, women, children, members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, people with disabilities, industrial workers, victims of disaster and people below an income limit set by each state can get free legal help. Legal services include advice and help before any authority, so they can cover a claim, a hearing or an appeal about the roll. Ask at the District Legal Services Authority at the district court, or call the NALSA helpline on 15100. In Bihar in September 2025 the Supreme Court had the legal services authorities send para-legal volunteers to help voters file claims and objections online.
Call 15100 or visit the District Legal Services Authority office at the district court.
Say that your name was left off the roll and what stage you are at (claim, hearing or appeal).
Take the notice or order you received and any documents you have.
Ask for a para-legal volunteer or panel lawyer to help you fill in the form or the appeal.
What the Supreme Court's orders give an elector

In Bihar the Court had the roughly 65 lakh names left off the draft published booth by booth, with the reason for each, searchable by EPIC number and put up at panchayat and block offices. It allowed claims with a copy of Aadhaar and then made Aadhaar the twelfth document, as proof of identity. In West Bengal it let people flagged for discrepancies file through an authorised representative, gave them ten more days, and set up appellate tribunals of former judges for those whose claims judicial officers rejected. Its judgment of 27 May 2026 upheld the revision and said that people in Bihar whose names were, in its words, "erroneously deleted" as absent, dead, shifted or duplicate may challenge the decision in court.
Search the list of names left off by your EPIC number on the district or Chief Electoral Officer's website, or look at the panchayat or block notice board.
Note the reason given against your name. It tells you what to answer.
Aadhaar can be given as proof of identity. It is not accepted as proof of citizenship.
In West Bengal, a rejected claim goes to the appellate tribunal. A pending appeal did not give a right to vote at the 2026 poll.
Going to court

An elector can ask the High Court, under Article 226 of the Constitution, to review a decision on the roll. The Supreme Court's judgment of 27 May 2026 says the Commission's enquiry into eligibility remains open to judicial review, and that people in Bihar whose names were, in its words, "erroneously deleted" as absent, dead, shifted or duplicate may challenge the decision that way. On 11 November 2025, while it was hearing the challenges to the revision, the Supreme Court asked the High Courts to hold back cases on whether the revision was valid. That request did not cover an elector's own case about his or her own entry. The judgment of 27 May 2026 decided the petitions about Bihar, and the petition in which the request was made is not among the cases it lists.
Use the claim, the hearing and both appeals first, and keep every order.
If you still have no remedy, ask the District Legal Services Authority for a lawyer to file a writ petition in the High Court.
